What British paramountcy meant

As the East India Company expanded, it increasingly claimed that its authority was superior to that of Indian states.

This claim became known as British paramountcy. The policy is particularly associated with Lord Hastings, Governor-General from 1813 to 1823.

Paramountcy

Paramountcy was the British claim that their political authority was supreme in relation to Indian states. The Company used this claim to justify interference in their affairs and, where it considered necessary, the threat or use of annexation.

Paramountcy did not mean that every princely state was immediately annexed. Some states remained under their own rulers while accepting British supremacy. Others were absorbed into directly administered territory.

The Doctrine of Lapse

Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General from 1848 to 1856, implemented a policy known as the Doctrine of Lapse.

Under this policy, the Company refused to recognise succession by an adopted heir in certain dependent princely states when a ruler died without a natural male heir. The Company could then declare that the ruler's state had lapsed and annex its territory.

Adoption was an established practice in Indian ruling families. The Company's refusal to recognise an adopted successor for political succession could therefore deprive a ruling dynasty of its state despite the existence of an adopted heir.

The doctrine was applied selectively to states over which the Company claimed the relevant authority. It should not be understood as an automatic rule governing every kingdom in India.

Important states annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse

StateYearBasis of annexation
Satara1848Doctrine of Lapse.
Sambalpur1850Doctrine of Lapse.
Udaipur1852Doctrine of Lapse.
Nagpur1853Doctrine of Lapse.
Jhansi1854Doctrine of Lapse.

In this list, Udaipur refers to the smaller princely state associated with the central Indian region, not the well-known Mewar kingdom centred on Udaipur in Rajasthan.

The annexation of Jhansi was especially important because the refusal to recognise the adopted heir affected the ruling family. Rani Lakshmibai later became a prominent leader of resistance during the uprising of 1857.

Awadh was annexed on a different pretext

The Company annexed Awadh in 1856 under Dalhousie.

Unlike Jhansi or Nagpur, Awadh was not annexed through the Doctrine of Lapse. The Company justified the takeover by alleging misgovernment by the Nawab.

The Nawab of Awadh was removed from power, and the state was brought under direct Company administration.

The annexation caused resentment among members of the ruling establishment, soldiers and sections of the population. This discontent contributed to the wider uprising of 1857.

Awadh and Jhansi: different reasons

  • Jhansi, 1854: Annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse.
  • Awadh, 1856: Annexed on the stated ground of misgovernment.

Different methods of expanding British control

British territorial expansion was not the result of a single policy. The Company combined military operations, treaties, political pressure and annexation.

MethodMeaningExample
Political interventionInfluencing or replacing an Indian ruler.Mir Jafar after Plassey, 1757.
Military conquestDefeating an Indian state through war.Punjab, 1849.
Subsidiary allianceRestricting independence through a protection treaty.Hyderabad, 1798.
Doctrine of LapseRefusing certain adopted succession claims.Jhansi, 1854.
Alleged misgovernmentAnnexation justified by criticism of a ruler's administration.Awadh, 1856.

The overall transformation from trading company to territorial power

By the middle of the 19th century, the English East India Company had moved far beyond its original commercial role.

Its rise involved several connected developments:

  1. European trading companies established coastal commercial bases and competed for Indian goods.
  2. Naval strength and treaties increased their commercial influence.
  3. The Company intervened in regional Indian politics and gained decisive influence in Bengal after Plassey.
  4. The victory at Buxar and the Diwani grant gave the Company major military and financial advantages.
  5. Wars against Mysore, the Marathas and the Sikhs weakened major Indian powers.
  6. Subsidiary alliances, paramountcy and annexations extended direct and indirect British control.

The Company therefore gained power through a combination of trade, military force, diplomatic agreements, revenue rights and political intervention. These methods were related, but they were not identical.

Prelims focus

  • Lord Hastings is associated with the policy of paramountcy.
  • Lord Dalhousie served as Governor-General from 1848 to 1856.
  • Satara was annexed in 1848 under the Doctrine of Lapse.
  • Nagpur was annexed in 1853; Jhansi in 1854.
  • Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the stated ground of misgovernment.
  • Trap: Paramountcy, subsidiary alliance and Doctrine of Lapse were distinct instruments of British expansion.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, pp. 15–20, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 10, Eighteenth-Century Political Formations, pp. 138–151, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, Rise of Regional Powers, Unit 1, Section 1.5, The Rise of British Power, consulted 20 November 2026.]
